quotes.t: On Being and the One is a brief position paper examining whether the One is prior to being, as the Neoplatonists had taught, or coincident with it, as Aristotle had argued. Pico della Mirandola takes the Aristotelian side, utilizing a …

rel.basis: Allen says De ente takes the Aristotelian side, presents a basically Thomist position, and dismisses the Parmenides and Sophist as dialectical games; Sudduth says Pico sets out to reconcile the Aristotelian identity of one and being with the Platonist priority of the one, i.e. to find both sides right rather than to take one.

Howlett agrees the view is apparently Aristotelian but adds that Pico argues it is also Plato's own original perspective, later misinterpreted by his followers, so the treatise claims both sides rather than taking Aristotle's.
Miller says there can be no doubt Pico's metaphysic of existence came from Thomas; Allen says De ente presents a basically Thomist position using Aquinas's distinctions on essence and existence.

Allen's claim that Pico's dismissal of the Parmenides and Sophist annoyed Ficino, who called it temerity, is borne out by Miller's report that Ficino's own Parmenides commentary directly replies that Pico's interpretation is against the opinion of all the Platonists.

Allen's programmatic claim that Pico scholars have missed Ficino's role in generating De ente and the reaction to it depends on his own prior claim that the treatise's dismissal of the Parmenides and Sophist specifically annoyed Ficino.

Edelheit reports Allen's conclusion that Ficino emerges as a good deal more original than Pico in interpreting the Parmenides, against Klibansky, which sits against Allen's own separate claim that Pico's dismissal of the dialogue was itself an act of scholarly boldness that annoyed Ficino.

Allen reports that Ficino was 'annoyed' at Pico's dismissal of the Parmenides and Sophist and called it 'temerity'; Howlett's observation that Ficino's collected letters contain no letter about, or mention of, De ente qualifies the evidentiary basis of that annoyance -- it is attested only in Ficino's Parmenides commentary, not in his surviving correspondence.

Howlett reports Lohr's argument 'that Pico is attacking Ficino through Aquinas' distinction between these different types of being'; Allen independently says Pico's De ente 'utiliz[es] a number of subtle distinctions from Aquinas concerning essence and existence' on 'a basically Thomist basis' and that this 'annoyed Ficino' -- both identify the deployment of Thomist ontology as the mechanism of the anti-Ficino argument.

judged.justification: Concise statement of the disagreement in terms of Parmenides/Sophist status and Thomist essence-existence distinctions.
